explain.say: Switch on a big motor, like a lift or a workshop saw, and the lights can dip for a moment. Why? On the board, a DC motor with 0.5 ohms of armature resistance has just been connected to 24 volts. It is not turning yet, so only that small resistance limits the current: 24 over 0.5, a whopping 48 amps.

explain.say: Here is a DC machine in 3D. Spin this same machine with an engine and it becomes a generator: the armature coils cut the field and a voltage appears at the brushes. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

draw.text: DC generators and back EMF: why a spinning motor pushes back on its supply

explain.say: Now flip the idea. Turn the same machine with an engine or a turbine, and the coil cuts through the magnetic field, so a voltage is induced in it: it has become a generator. That voltage, E, equals k phi times the speed omega. Our machine has k phi of 0.5, so at 40 radians per second it makes 20 volts. What happens to E if it spins twice as fast?

parts.label: Armature coil
parts.ask: How does a DC generator make voltage?

explain.say: E doubles. And here is the key: a motor is also a generator, even while it is motoring. As it speeds up it makes a voltage that opposes the supply, called back EMF. At 40 radians per second the back EMF is 20 volts, leaving only 4 volts across the resistance, so the current falls to 8 amps. Watch the ammeter. What decides how fast the motor finally runs?

explain.say: It speeds up until the back EMF leaves just enough current for the load torque. Now push it faster, say an electric car rolling downhill. At 52 radians per second the back EMF is 26 volts, more than the supply, so current flows backwards, 4 amps, charging the battery. That is regenerative braking. What does the motor feel while it charges?

explain.say: A braking torque that slows the car. So back EMF is the motor's built-in regulator, and it explains the dipping lights: at start-up there is none. That is why big motors get starters that add resistance, like 2.5 ohms to hold the start current to 8 amps, or ramp up the voltage. Excellent! faq.q: What is back EMF in a DC motor?
faq.a: As the armature spins in the field it acts as a generator, inducing a voltage that opposes the supply. This back EMF equals k phi times speed, and the current is supply voltage minus back EMF, divided by the armature resistance.
asks: Why does a spinning motor generate voltage?

faq.q: Why does a motor draw a huge current when it starts?
faq.a: At standstill there is no back EMF, so only the small armature resistance limits the current. A 24 volt motor with 0.5 ohms draws 48 amps at the instant of starting, and this falls as it speeds up.

faq.q: How does a DC generator make voltage?
faq.a: When the armature coil is turned through the magnetic field, the changing flux through it induces a voltage, E equals k phi omega. The commutator turns the alternating coil voltage into DC at the brushes.

When the wheels drive the motor fast enough that its back EMF exceeds the supply voltage, the current reverses. The machine then works as a generator, charging the battery and producing a braking torque.
asks: How do electric cars recover energy when braking?

faq.q: What is the DC motor voltage equation?
faq.a: V equals E plus I times R a: the supply voltage is shared between the back EMF and the drop across the armature resistance. Rearranged, the current equals V minus E, over R a.
asks: What is V = E + IR for a motor?

facts: A DC machine's EMF is E = kΦω: proportional to speed for a fixed field.
Electric and hybrid cars use regenerative braking to recover part of their kinetic energy.
Without back EMF, a motor's starting current is limited only by its winding resistance.

quiz.say: A 24 volt DC motor with 0.5 ohms of armature resistance runs with 22 volts of back EMF. What current does it draw?
quiz.show: A 24 V DC motor with a 0.5 Ω armature runs with 22 V back EMF. What current does it draw?
quiz.why: I equals V minus E over R: 24 minus 22 is 2 volts, and 2 over 0.5 ohms is 4 amps.

wrong.1: 48 amps is the starting current, when there is no back EMF.
wrong.2: That divides the back EMF by the resistance instead of the difference.
